issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding triggers are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another in a car accident, given the rest of the profile centers on crash-related and guilt/shame themes. This trigger introduces a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Feelings' is internally incoherent as worded: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of avoidance. Within the maladaptive strategies node, it directly conflicts with an avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' fits poorly with the rest of the profile for a perpetration-type accident trauma in which the patient's appraisals otherwise center on guilt, humiliation, and shattered beliefs. There are no memory, trigger, or strategy items suggesting bodily injury, panic/somatic threat, or physical incapacity to support this appraisal.

vignette:
Rajan Mehta had been a careful, methodical 42-year-old tax inspector, the kind of man who prided himself on order, evidence, and doing things by the book. That certainty had been shattered on a rainy evening drive home from work, when a momentary misjudgment at an intersection left one car broadside and its driver seriously injured. He replayed the scene endlessly in the first hours afterward: the sickening jolt, the sound that followed, and then the scene at the roadside as people gathered while he stood frozen, sick with the knowledge that he had done this. Since then, certain moments had acquired a brutal force. Seeing cars hit by accident, hearing about crashes on the news, or even passing a wreck on the roadside would make his stomach clench and send him searching for some way to blunt the feeling. At funerals, in cemeteries, or at grief-filled family gatherings, where the air itself seemed charged with loss, he felt the same tightening in his chest and would try hard not to think about the trauma, telling himself to push it away before it overwhelmed him. He had also become intensely wary of talking about what happened; even a routine question from his wife or a colleague could leave him visibly tense, as though the event were still waiting just beneath the surface.

What Rajan could not escape was the way the memory itself kept intruding. Some parts of that evening remained locked in with punishing clarity - the rain on the windshield, the angle of the other car, the echo of voices - while other stretches were blank, so incomplete that he felt he was only remembering fragments and the rest was missing. When he tried to recall it, he sometimes heard in his head the same sounds he had heard at the scene, as if the moment had never really ended. Those broken, sensory memories fed his conviction that he had destroyed something irreparable. He had come to believe that his beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed, because a world in which one mistake could leave another person gravely harmed no longer felt stable or fair to him. He was haunted by the thought that he should have protected others and failed, and that failure felt not temporary but permanent. The humiliation of it sat on him constantly; he felt permanently humiliated by what happened, as if everyone who knew the story could see through him.

When the memories surged, Rajan's reactions began to shape the way he thought and moved through the world. He would tell himself he deserved to suffer because of what happened, and that self-punishment made the shame deepen into something darker and more absolute. At the same time, he tried to soothe himself by reminding himself it could have been worse, that the other driver had survived, that the consequences had not been fatal. But even that downward comparison rarely helped for long. Instead, it left him feeling briefly guilty for seeking comfort at all, as though minimizing the harm were another moral failure. The more he tried to judge himself into endurance, the more certain he became that he was fundamentally disgraced and unworthy, and that he had no right to be relieved. Those beliefs kept the event alive in his mind: every flash of memory seemed to confirm that he was the sort of man who had failed when it mattered most.

In the months that followed, the triggers and the inner punishment fed one another. A sudden image of cars colliding, a passing ambulance, or an invitation to a funeral would send him back into the same loop of self-condemnation, and in response he would clamp down harder, trying not to think about the trauma and forcing himself to move on. Yet each attempt to suppress it made the memories return with greater force, often in the middle of work at the tax office when he was reviewing files or sitting through long, quiet stretches at his desk. He found himself distracted by the fear that something like that crash could happen again, and the old images would rise so quickly that he would avoid the subject entirely. He stopped lingering over conversations about road safety, declined an uncle's invitation to a memorial service, and took longer routes home to avoid the intersection where the accident had occurred. His avoidance shrank his world and made him more isolated from his wife, who noticed how carefully he sidestepped any mention of the event.

By the time he came for help, Rajan was exhausted by the effort of holding the whole thing at bay. The more he fought the memories, the more they seemed to attack him in fragments and sounds, and the more certain he felt that he deserved the misery that followed. He feared that if he kept going like this, he would never be able to speak about the crash without falling apart, and he worried that the humiliation would never lift. What finally brought him in was the sense that he could no longer keep functioning at work or at home without flinching from every reminder. He hoped, with considerable reluctance, that therapy might help him face the event without feeling condemned by it, but what frightened him most was the possibility that remembering fully would confirm the worst thing he already believed about himself.
